name: Mother Ione
appearance: The Prior of Saint Ysolde's, in her seventies: small and very upright, white hair cropped close under a plain linen coif, a soft round face creased like a winter apple, and pale eyes that count everyone in a room in turn. The creases run all over it: rosy cheeks, sparse white brows, very pale grey-blue eyes, and a small firm mouth that keeps a faint, patient smile. The coif is tied under her chin, and she wears a high-collared gown of plain grey-brown wool under a worn grey-green wool shawl. Gentle in face and manner, with iron under it. In the warming room she has the one good chair by the fire and offers it to nobody.
portrait_alt: Portrait of Mother Ione: a small old woman in her seventies with a round, deeply creased face, rosy cheeks, very pale grey-blue eyes, sparse white brows and a faint, patient smile, white hair under a plain white linen coif tied under her chin, in a high-collared grey-brown wool gown and a worn grey-green shawl, sitting in a carved high-backed wooden chair in a stone room with a hearth fire burning beside her.
last_seen_doing: Came out of the chapel unasked and stood beside the Captain under the tower while he said the verse, then at the bars; told the Confessor the almoner is a brother of the House under the law of guests, older than the Crown's, and that his name is not the Captain's to give; put her own roof under the night's answer; at the cot after the night lamps asked the Captain what the House is for.
now: In the chapel doorway with the rain on her coif, having asked the Captain what the House is for. The dawn's answer comes from under her roof, by her own word to the Confessor.
story_so_far: She turned a key no Prior before her had turned, three nights running, and asked at the top of the stair only whether the Captain came up on his own leg. When they came up with his hand white she looked, and asked nothing.

quote.text: I have never once given a name to a writ. Did you think I would start with yours?

known_facts.fact: By the time Wren Ashdown reached the infirmary hall with word of the grey cloaks on the Holloway, Mother Ione had been told.
known_facts.evidence: Mother Ione's been told.

known_facts.fact: She holds her council in the warming room off the cloister, has the one good chair by the fire, and offers it to nobody.

She asked Rae Thorne how the list was read, had Maelis give Darrow the law of Old Mercy, and asked Sister Pell whether she would ring it dawn and dusk for as long as the grey cloaks care to sit at the bottom.

She has not yet decided whether Old Mercy rings. She called Darrow back from the stair to ask what he would have her know first, and what the lay brothers should tell the valley when it asks who sleeps up here.
known_facts.evidence: Before I decide whether Old Mercy rings, is there anything you'd have me know?

known_facts.fact: She let the Captain ask to be sent down and the Mender answer him, then closed the council having heard them all: Sister Pell would hear from her before dusk, and the lay brothers would want to know what to say to the valley.
known_facts.evidence: you'll hear from me before dusk

known_facts.fact: At her council she put it to Darrow as a question: if the lay brothers tell the valley there's nobody up here, what does a sanctuary bell tell it at dusk? After his answer, Old Mercy did not ring at dusk, nor at the next dawn.
known_facts.evidence: what does a sanctuary bell tell it at dusk?

known_facts.fact: When Darrow offered to go down on the cage so the list would have nothing to climb for, she asked him how many names the next writ would carry once the House had given them one, and did not wait for him to count.
known_facts.evidence: how many will the next writ carry?

known_facts.fact: She came up the hall on the last stroke of the dawn bell and waited at the foot of Darrow's cot until Benedek's lips stopped moving before she spoke.
known_facts.evidence: She waited until they stopped.

known_facts.fact: At first light the winch-brothers went down with Darrow's story of the far side of the mountain, to tell it at the winch-house fire, so that the valley would have it by noon.
known_facts.evidence: with your story of the far side of the mountain

known_facts.fact: She asked Darrow whether he told it for the House or for the river; he said the river had had enough of them.
known_facts.evidence: or for the river?

known_facts.fact: At the next dawn she told Darrow Old Mercy had not rung at dusk, so the valley heard what it always hears from the House; when he said there was no law on the gate, she said not till she rings, and asked whether he had slept any worse for it.
known_facts.evidence: Did you sleep any worse for it?

known_facts.fact: She asked Darrow, who reads a line before it moves, to tell Wren when, once the grey cloaks are at the bars; it was not a question, and he said he would.
known_facts.evidence: will you tell Wren when?

known_facts.fact: She ordered nobody into the court; at the hour bell she asked whether the House would like to see who had climbed so far to read to it, and the House came.
known_facts.evidence: the House had come

known_facts.fact: She stood before the gate with Maelis a pace behind her shoulder; when the Confessor said she would forgive him if he read anyway, she asked, 'Would I stop you?'
known_facts.evidence: Would I stop you?

known_facts.fact: She let the Confessor hold his paper out through the bars while the bell did not come; when he said he would hate to tell the bell-houses her House broke the law of guests to keep a courier standing in the cold, she asked the gate-ward whether they should take the Confessor's paper.
known_facts.evidence: shall we take the Confessor's paper?

known_facts.fact: When Old Mercy rang she told the Confessor, without moving and lowering her voice so the court leaned to hear, that while it rings no blade climbs the Steps or passes the gate, and the other half, which his order reads at every bell-house twice over: no name under it is taken down against its will.
known_facts.evidence: no name under it is taken down against its will

known_facts.fact: When Darrow gave his name at the bars and the Confessor thanked her for her candour, she did not look at the gate; she looked at Darrow and asked him whether the shoulder was hurt.
known_facts.evidence: She asked him whether the shoulder was hurt.

known_facts.fact: Every night, alone in the chapel, she says the names of everyone under the House's roof, and notices which ones she has had to stop saying.
known_facts.evidence: Everyone under this roof, every night

known_facts.fact: Asked to be angry that Darrow buried the House's story at the gate, she asked whose story it was: he gave it to the lay brothers, she only let them carry it, and a lie told for a man is his to bury.
known_facts.evidence: A lie told for a man is his to bury

known_facts.fact: She told him the Menders' vow is four words, to mend what climbs, and nobody who wrote it thought to add 'and hand it down to whoever asks'; she has never once given a name to a writ.
known_facts.evidence: To mend what climbs.

known_facts.fact: She said she held the bell so that Darrow would have a choice too, and that he is in her count of names, and was before he gave his name to the Confessor.
known_facts.evidence: I held the bell so that you would have one too.

known_facts.fact: Asked for the Mender at the bars, she answered: We are a House of Menders; which of us did you climb for?
known_facts.evidence: Which of us did you climb for?

known_facts.fact: The undercroft key came to her from the Prior before her, and to her from the one before; none of them has turned it.
known_facts.evidence: None of us has turned it.

known_facts.fact: She neither forbade nor permitted the door.
known_facts.evidence: I haven't said yes.

known_facts.fact: She asked what he would do at the bottom of a stair he cannot come back up by himself, and who would carry him up.
known_facts.evidence: a stair you cannot come back up by yourself

known_facts.fact: She will call every soul under her roof who can stand into the hall after the night bell to hear what he found.
known_facts.evidence: After the night bell I'll call the House into this hall

known_facts.fact: Because he gave his name at her gate without asking her, she asked him whether he would like to be the one who tells the House.
known_facts.evidence: Would you like to be the one who tells them?

known_facts.fact: She gave the Captain the House and no other help in telling it.
known_facts.evidence: that was all the help she meant to give him

known_facts.fact: She wears a key on a cord at her neck, black and long and older than any on her ring.
known_facts.evidence: A key hung on it, black and long, older than any on her ring.

known_facts.fact: She told the Captain to ask her for it when he can say what he would do at the bottom.
known_facts.evidence: When you can tell me what you'd do at the bottom

known_facts.fact: She told the Captain to come to her with what he would do at the bottom of the stair when the Mender tells him.
known_facts.evidence: And when she tells you," said the Prior, "come and tell me what you'd do at the bottom.

known_facts.fact: The masons found the undercroft stair when they cut the House's footings, and built on it rather than through it.
known_facts.evidence: They built on it, not through it.

known_facts.fact: The Prior before her gave her the key with the ring and told her to wear it; neither of the two Priors before her turned it.
known_facts.evidence: She never turned it. Nor did hers.

known_facts.fact: She turned the key at dusk, with both hands.
known_facts.evidence: She put both hands to it, and it went over with a sound like a knuckle.

known_facts.fact: She will hear what he saw below when he knows what it was.
known_facts.evidence: You'll tell me what you saw when you know what it was.

known_facts.fact: She came down the row, looked at the hand and the mortar on the linen press, and asked nothing at all.
known_facts.evidence: and asked nothing at all

known_facts.fact: She counted the nights between his promise at the stair head and his telling: two.
known_facts.evidence: I counted the nights between. Two.

known_facts.fact: She says every name under the roof in the chapel every night, has not had to stop saying one since he came, and will go on saying all of them.
known_facts.evidence: I say every name under this roof in this chapel every night, Captain, and I have not had to stop saying one since you came. I shall go on saying all of them.

known_facts.fact: She told the Confessor that the almoner came up the Steps unarmed years ago and was warmed and fed, the law of guests, and that a guest the House has kept that long is the House's.
known_facts.evidence: A guest the House has kept that long is the House's.

known_facts.fact: She said the almoner's name is not the Captain's to give.
known_facts.evidence: You'll not have his name from the Captain, because it isn't the Captain's to give.

known_facts.fact: She asked the Captain what the House is for, so that it was not a question.
known_facts.evidence: "What is the House for, Captain?"

relationships.label: the Confessor who read his list at her gate
relationships.note: She let him read, made him wait at the wicket for the bell, and answered his men with the bell and the law of names; when the Captain gave his name, Marrant thanked her for her candour.
